6Attention

Attention = each word takes its query card (Q), compares it with every word’s key card (K), then mixes their value cards (V) in proportion.

ⓘ Notes
Attention = each word takes its query card (Q), compares it with every word’s key card (K), then mixes their value cards (V) in proportion.

Why it’s designed this way: “Whom to look at” isn’t a hard-coded rule but learned from data; all words can be computed at once, so it’s fast.

On this page:

🧒 In plain words first

Attention is like finding books in a library: you hold a question (the query card Q), compare it with the label on each book’s spine (the key card K), and the better a book matches, the more carefully you read its contents (the value card V). Every word “searches” the other words of the sentence this way.

Training means drilling the model on huge amounts of text with “guess the next word” exercises: after each guess the answer is checked, the more wrong it was the bigger the penalty (the loss), and then every parameter is nudged a tiny bit in the direction that lowers the penalty. Repeat billions to trillions of times.

At first the parameters are random, so the model is basically guessing, and even leans towards “bad”.

Loss = −log(probability of the correct word): giving the right answer 70% means a loss of about 0.36; giving it only 10% means about 2.3.

Tap the cards below to see why the three training essentials are designed this way and why they work:

Massive data + next-word guessing

The training exercises: cut a passage from text and guess the word that follows.

Loss (cross-entropy)

A single number: how badly this question was guessed.

Backpropagation + gradient descent

Works out which way each parameter should move, then takes a small step.

Note: real training adjusts all parameters (thousands up to hundreds of billions of numbers in all kinds of tables); the scores only change as a result. To keep it intuitive, this demo pushes the scores directly. Also, during training every position in a sentence guesses its own next word at the same time (a “mask” stops it from peeking at the answer), so one sentence is many exercises at once.
Inside the Transformer block:
② Diagram

Go deeper (the full explanation)

Each word prepares three cards: a query card Q (what I’m looking for), a key card K (what I am, for others to match against) and a value card V (the information I hand over when attended to). Like in a library: you hold your question (Q) against each book’s spine label (K), and the better it matches, the more closely you read that book’s content (V).

Score = multiply Q and K position by position and add up (dot product), then divide by √2 (2 is the card length). Masking = set the scores of “later words” to minus infinity, which becomes 0% after softmax.

③ Details · why

🧒 In plain words first

One person sees things only one way, so attention has many groups looking at once (multiple heads), each with its own eyes, and what they all see is put together at the end.

Go deeper (the full explanation)

To be more exact…People say “some heads watch grammar, some watch who ‘it’ refers to”, but that is only a picture: how the heads divide the work forms by itself during training, and many heads are hard to explain.

  • One set of Q/K/V tables can only learn one “way of looking”.
  • So attention has many sets (“heads”, often dozens)
  • each runs steps ①–④ above on its own with its own Q/K/V tables, and at the end the results of all heads are concatenated and multiplied by an output table to merge them back to the original length.
  • People often describe heads as “one watches grammar, one watches references (who ‘it’ is), one watches neighbouring words” — but that’s only an analogy
  • the division of labour emerges in training, and many heads are hard to interpret.
③ Details · why

🧒 In plain words first

Why this design? There are three cards because “what am I looking for”, “how can I be found” and “what do I hand over once found” are three different things. How well two cards match is worked out by multiplying position by position and adding up; longer cards give bigger numbers, so the result is scaled down first to keep the shares from being lopsided. The later words are covered up: the job is to guess the next word, and peeking would be copying the answer.

Go deeper (the full explanation)
In one line: three roles Q/K/V (what I’m looking for / how I’m found / what I hand over) → Q·K dot product as relevance → ÷√length to keep proportions from getting extreme → masking forbids peeking at the answer → softmax turns scores into proportions with a fixed total → mix V by those proportions → multi-head looks several ways at once.
Q table (makes query cards)Turns a word vector into a “query card”: what kind of word am I looking for?

🧠 Why it’s designed this way (the logic underneath)

A word needs different features when it is “looking for others” and when it is “being looked for”. A separate Q table translates word vectors specifically into “what I’m looking for”.

✅ Why this works

Training adjusts the Q table so that truly useful words get higher match scores: the gradient rewards ways of asking that “look at the right people”.

⚠️ Limits / notes: “Query card” is only an analogy; the numbers in Q usually have no readable meaning.

K table (makes key cards)Turns a word vector into a “key card”: what kind of word I am, for others to match against.

🧠 Why it’s designed this way (the logic underneath)

“What I am, and how I’m found” is a different role, so it gets its own K table. If Q and K used the same table, each word’s match with itself would be naturally inflated, and asymmetric relations like “I’m looking for action words, but I myself am a noun” couldn’t be expressed.

✅ Why this works

With Q and K learned separately, the matching can be asymmetric: “apples” paying close attention to “eating” doesn’t mean “eating” pays the same attention to “apples”.

⚠️ Limits / notes: “Key card” is only an analogy.

V table (makes value cards)Turns a word vector into a “value card”: the information I hand over when others attend to me.

🧠 Why it’s designed this way (the logic underneath)

“Whether I get looked at” (K) and “what I hand over when looked at” (V) are different things: the features used for matching aren’t necessarily the information most worth passing on.

✅ Why this works

Each of the three roles has its own table, each trained into the shape that suits its role best, which makes the model more flexible.

⚠️ Limits / notes: This is a plain-language description of common practice; actual implementations vary by system.

① ScoreMatch query cards against key cards to compute match scores.

🧠 Why it’s designed this way (the logic underneath)

We need a number for “how well a query card matches a key card”. The dot product is the simplest: the more aligned, the larger, and one matrix multiplication computes all pairs of words at once. Then divide by √(card length): the longer the card, the larger and more variable the dot product naturally is, and without scaling softmax would become extreme (almost 100% on one word).

✅ Why this works

  • When the proportions are too extreme the gradient approaches 0 (vanishing gradients) and the model stops learning
  • after scaling the scores stay in a suitable range, the proportions don’t go “all in” from the start, and the training signal flows smoothly.
  • The meaning of high or low dot products is, again, given by training: the Q and K tables are tuned so that “words that deserve attention” get higher dot products.

⚠️ Limits / notes: √length comes from a simple statistical estimate (when the numbers are random and independent, the spread of the dot product is about √length), and works very well in practice.

② Mask (look back only)Only itself and earlier words may be seen; no peeking at later ones.

🧠 Why it’s designed this way (the logic underneath)

The task is guessing the next word, and the answer is right after it. In training the whole sentence is laid out, so allowing a look ahead would mean copying the answer and learning nothing real. Besides, in use the later words don’t exist yet; training and use must have the same conditions.

✅ Why this works

Once masked, every position in a sentence can serve at the same time as an exercise that “only sees the text before it”, which makes training very efficient; the skills learned apply unchanged in use.

⚠️ Limits / notes: This is how “generative” models work; models built for understanding tasks, such as BERT, don’t mask the later words and use a different kind of exercise.

③ softmax weightsTurns match scores into attention weights that add up to 100%.

🧠 Why it’s designed this way (the logic underneath)

The match scores need to become “shares”: all non-negative with a fixed total of 100%. That way, however many words come before, the mixed result stays in the same range instead of growing with the number of words.

✅ Why this works

High scores are amplified and low scores suppressed, so the model can “focus” attention on a few key words; and it is differentiable everywhere, so training can smoothly adjust “look at whom a bit more”.

⚠️ Limits / notes: A fixed total of 1 means attention has to be spent even when no word is particularly relevant; research has found models “park” surplus attention on positions like the beginning.

④ Weighted mixMixes everyone’s value cards into one new card according to the attention weights.

🧠 Why it’s designed this way (the logic underneath)

The simplest way to gather information is a weighted average of everyone’s value cards by attention share: the more relevant, the bigger the contribution.

✅ Why this works

The result is a new piece of information as long as the original vector, which can be added straight back to it (the residual); the whole process is differentiable, so training can tell the V table “what to hand over”.

⚠️ Limits / notes: A weighted average is itself linear; more complex processing relies on the feed-forward network that follows.

⑤ Concat headsSeveral attention groups run at once and their results are joined end to end.

🧠 Why it’s designed this way (the logic underneath)

One set of Q/K/V can only produce one set of attention shares, but a word often needs to track several relations at once: grammatical pairings, references (who “it” is), neighbouring words… Multi-head = running several sets in parallel, each looking its own way.

✅ Why this works

Each head uses shorter cards, so the total computation is about the same as one big head, yet it can capture several attention patterns at once, and the concatenated information is richer.

⚠️ Limits / notes: “Heads specialize naturally” is an empirical observation: many heads are hard to interpret, and some research finds removing some heads matters little; why and how they specialize is still being researched.

⑥ Output tableMerges the concatenated multi-head results and brings them back to the original length.

🧠 Why it’s designed this way (the logic underneath)

After concatenation the heads’ findings are just “sitting side by side”; a table is needed to mix them and bring them back to the original length so they can be added to the original vector.

✅ Why this works

Here the heads’ information can combine; the output length matches the original vector, which is what makes the residual addition work.

⚠️ Limits / notes: This is a plain-language description of common practice; actual implementations vary by system.

③ Details · why

🧒 In plain words first

Attention on its own cannot tell which word comes first. RoPE’s trick is like turning the hands of a clock: the later a word sits, the further its card is turned. After both cards are turned, comparing them depends only on how many words apart they are, not on where they sit.

Go deeper (the full explanation)

Attention scores alone don’t know word order. Rotary position embedding (RoPE) rotates Q and K by a position-dependent angle before scoring.

  • Pair i turns at θᵢ = 10000^(−2i/d): early pairs turn fast, later pairs slowly.
  • After both vectors are rotated, their dot product depends only on the distance m − n.

🧪 Attention playground: swap words, toggle masking, change the head count

🧒 In plain words first

Swap some words, switch “look back only” on and off, change how many groups are looking, and tap a row of the heat map to see whom that word is looking at (the patterns are made up by rule).

ⓘ Sample data: attention patterns are rule-based

  • Why it’s built this way: A word’s meaning depends on its context (who is “it”?).
  • Attention lets each word mix in other words’ information according to how relevant they are
  • masking guarantees it can’t peek ahead
  • multiple heads let the model look several ways at once.
Tap a row of the heatmap to see whom that word looks at
👀 Try this:
  • select the last word (“too slow” / “too fast”) and see where the “find the reference” head points — switch it and the pointer moves.
  • Then tap the “it” row: with masking on it can’t yet see the words after it, so it hedges between both
  • with masking off it can “peek” ahead and decide directly — but during generation the later words don’t exist yet, so real models must mask.
  • Set the head count to 1: the different relations get blurred into one average.
🧪 LabIllustrative

🧪 RoPE: shift both positions, the score stays

🧒 In plain words first

m is the query card’s position, n the key card’s position, and s moves both along by the same amount. Moving s leaves the score unchanged, because the gap m − n between them stays the same.

ⓘ The 4-dimensional Q and K values are illustrative; the rotation (θ = 1 and 0.01, i.e. 10000^(−2i/d) for d = 4) and the dot product are exact.

Why it’s built this way:
  • The score depends only on m − n, so the model learns “how far apart”, not “at which word”.
👀 Try this:
  • Drag only the shift: the two scores stay identical.
  • Set m = n: the score equals the plain, unrotated dot product.
